title: Why You'd Never Survive a Swim in Europa's Ocean
screen_title: Why You'd Never Survive a Swim in Europa's Ocean
subtitle: The hidden ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon
yt_title: Why You'd Never Survive a Swim in Europa's Ocean
intro: What would happen if you tried to swim in the hidden ocean of Europa, Jupiter's icy moon? We land on ice colder than Antarctica under a sky full of Jupiter, survive (barely) the radiation, drill down through kilometers of ice, and sink into a dark ocean with twice as much water as all of Earth's seas. Stay to the end to find out what might be swimming down there, and when we'll finally find out.

segments.text: What if you dove into an alien ocean? First you'd have to survive the radiation on the surface. Then dig through more than ten kilometers of ice. And then, the real danger begins.

segments.text: Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we try to reach the most promising ocean beyond Earth. So, let's go.

files: Good Morning From the International Space Station.jpg
visual.query: Good Morning From the International Space Station

segments.text: This is Europa. One of the moons of Jupiter. It's a little smaller than our own Moon, and covered in a shell of cracked, brownish ice.

files: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited.jpg
visual.query: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited

segments.headline: Jupiter's icy moon

segments.text: But under that ice, scientists are confident there's an ocean. A real, salty, liquid water ocean, all the way around the moon.
segments.headline: A hidden ocean

segments.text: And it's huge. Europa's ocean may hold about twice as much water as all the oceans on Earth combined.

visual.label: the water in all of Earth's oceans

segments.text: Water is what life needs. That makes Europa one of the best places in the solar system to look for life. So let's go there. And stay to the end, because I'll show you what might be swimming in that dark ocean, and when we'll finally know.

visual.query: ISS-45 StoryOfWater, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

segments.headline: What lives there?

segments.text: First, getting there. Jupiter is, on average, about seven hundred and seventy-eight million kilometers from the Sun. More than five times farther than Earth.
segments.headline: Out to Jupiter

segments.text: NASA's Europa Clipper is making this trip right now. It launched in October 2024, on a Falcon Heavy rocket.
segments.headline: Europa Clipper

segments.text: It swung past Mars in 2025, and its path brings it back past Earth in December 2026, for one last boost. It will reach Jupiter in April 2030, more than five years after launch.
Now imagine you land on Europa. Step outside. The ground is pure ice, laced with long reddish-brown cracks that run for thousands of kilometers.
segments.headline: A cracked shell

segments.text: It's about minus one hundred sixty degrees Celsius at the equator. Even colder at the poles. At these temperatures, water ice is as hard as rock.
And look up. Jupiter hangs in the black sky, about twenty-four times wider than our full Moon. It never rises and never sets. It just hangs there, with its stripes and storms slowly turning.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: Jupiter fills the sky

segments.text: You'd see the other moons, too. Volcanic Io, giant Ganymede, cratered Callisto, drifting across the sky like small planets.

files: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno.png
visual.query: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno

segments.headline: Neighboring moons

segments.text: Look closer at the ground. There are almost no craters. That means the surface is young, maybe only forty to ninety million years old. Something keeps wiping it clean.

files: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited.jpg
visual.query: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited

segments.headline: Almost no craters

segments.text: In some places, the ice has broken into huge jumbled blocks, like icebergs frozen back into a sea. Scientists call it chaos terrain. Warm water from below may have melted the ice and let it refreeze.
segments.headline: Chaos terrain

segments.text: And those reddish-brown streaks? In 2019, the Hubble Space Telescope found that some of them contain ordinary table salt. Salt that may have come up from the ocean below. Europa's ocean may be leaking onto its surface.

A day here is short, by moon standards. Europa circles Jupiter in about three and a half days. And every orbit, Jupiter blocks out the Sun for a few hours, plunging you into a strange, starlit eclipse.
It's beautiful. But you can't stay long. Here's the first reason you'd never survive.
segments.headline: The invisible killer

segments.text: Jupiter has the most powerful magnetic field of any planet. It traps charged particles and whips them around at incredible speeds. Europa orbits right inside that storm of radiation.

files: Jupiter - Great Red Spot - PJ7-60 61 62 - Balanced (49803032983).png
visual.query: Jupiter - Great Red Spot - PJ7-60 61 62 - Balanced (49803032983)

segments.text: Standing on the surface, you'd receive about five sieverts of radiation every day. That's thousands of times more than a person gets in a year at home.

Without heavy shielding, you'd be dangerously sick within hours, and you'd receive a deadly dose in about a day. That's why Europa Clipper will only swoop past the moon, again and again, and then retreat to safety.
segments.headline: Swoop in, swoop out

segments.text: It's planned to make nearly fifty close flybys, some just twenty-five kilometers above the ice.
Quick question for you. Do you think there's life in Europa's ocean? Yes, no, or maybe? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Do you think there's life in Europa's ocean?

segments.text: So let's get out of the radiation, and go down. The ice is your shield. Just a few meters of it would block most of the radiation.
segments.headline: Into the ice

segments.text: But the shell is thick. Scientists estimate it's somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five kilometers thick in most places. That's two Mount Everests of solid ice.
Drilling through it would take enormous energy. Some engineers imagine a nuclear-heated probe, slowly melting its way down, for months or even years.

Why is the ocean liquid at all, so far from the Sun? Because Jupiter squeezes Europa. As it orbits, Jupiter's gravity stretches and flexes the moon, over and over. That kneading creates heat, deep inside.
segments.headline: Squeezed by Jupiter

segments.text: It's the same force that makes Europa's neighbor Io the most volcanic world in the solar system.

files: Tvashtar volcano on Io from New Horizons.jpg
visual.query: Tvashtar volcano on Io from New Horizons

segments.text: Now you break through. Your probe slides into the water. And it's completely dark. No sunlight has ever reached this place.
segments.headline: Total darkness

segments.text: Switch on your lights, and you might see tiny flakes of ice drifting past, like snow falling upward. The underside of the ice shell above you would be your sky. A ceiling of ice, ten or twenty kilometers thick, between you and the stars.
segments.headline: A ceiling of ice

segments.text: The water is salty, and just around its freezing point. Colder than any swimming pool, but liquid.
And it's deep. Europa's ocean may be sixty to one hundred and fifty kilometers deep. The deepest point in Earth's ocean is about eleven kilometers.
Europa's gravity is weak, but with that much ice and water above you, the pressure at the bottom could be more than at the bottom of the Mariana Trench. Swim down unprotected, and you'd be crushed.

visual.query: ISS-45 StoryOfWater, Great Barrier Reef, Australia

segments.headline: Deeper than the trench

segments.text: So between the cold, the radiation, the ice and the pressure, there's no way you could swim here. But maybe something else already does.

files: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited.jpg
visual.query: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited

segments.text: Now the payoff I promised. What might be swimming down there?
segments.headline: Life in the dark

segments.text: On Earth, at the bottom of the sea, there are hot vents where life thrives without any sunlight at all. Microbes eat chemicals that bubble out of the rocks. Shrimp, worms and crabs eat the microbes.

If Europa's rocky seafloor has vents like these, its ocean could have the same ingredients. Water, energy, and chemistry. Scientists think the ocean might even contain oxygen, made on the surface by radiation, and carried down through the ice.
segments.headline: The ingredients of life

segments.text: If life exists there, it would most likely be tiny. Microbes, not monsters. But finding even one living cell would be one of the biggest discoveries in human history. It would mean life began twice, in one solar system.
So when will we know? Europa Clipper won't land, and it won't look for life directly. Its job is to find out whether Europa could support life.
segments.headline: Is Europa habitable?

segments.text: It will measure the ice shell with radar, map the surface, and fly through any plumes of water that might be spraying into space. Hubble has seen hints of them.
segments.headline: Flying through plumes?

segments.text: Europe's JUICE spacecraft, launched in 2023, is also on its way, and is set to fly past Europa too in the early 2030s.

segments.text: Clipper even carries a message. A plate engraved with the word water in more than a hundred languages, and a poem.
segments.headline: A message in a bottle

segments.text: So here's my question. If you could, would you ride a submarine down into Europa's dark ocean? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you ride a submarine into Europa's ocean?

segments.text: Europa is the place you'd never survive a swim. But it may be the place where we finally learn that we are not alone.
